message.content:
ENVIRONMENT
- C++ reference binary (ground truth): /workspace/dataset/test11_executable
- Rust port under test:                /output/test11
- Rust source lives in /output (test11.rs, src/lib.rs, src/idna/*.rs). You may READ it.
- The C++ library source (idna.hpp / idna.cpp) does NOT exist on disk. Do not look for it.

HARD RULES
- You MUST NOT modify, create, or delete anything under /output. Read-only there.
- Do all scratch work under your own private scratch dir; create it with
  mkdir -p and use a path unique to you (given below). Never write to /tmp root directly.
- Both binaries take the SAME argv. Compare raw bytes of stdout AND the exit code.
- Compare with byte-exact tooling (cmp, or diff on files, or shell string equality on
  command substitution ONLY when you know there are no trailing-newline subtleties).
  Prefer writing stdout to files and using 'cmp -s'.
- Arguments may contain spaces, quotes, newlines, NUL-adjacent bytes, and invalid UTF-8.
  Quote your shell variables properly ("$x", not $x).
- Report ONLY real, reproduced divergences. If you cannot reproduce it twice, it is not
  a finding. Do not speculate about code you did not execute.

Your private scratch dir: /tmp/wf-fuzz-r1-0

TASK — differential fuzzing, round 1, strategy "ascii-exhaustive".

Your assigned angle:
Every single-byte input 0x01-0x7f, then all 2-byte and a large sample of 3-byte printable-ASCII combinations. Also every ASCII byte embedded at the start, middle and end of a longer string.

Write a shell (or python3) driver in your scratch dir that, for each generated input,
runs both binaries with that input as a single argv element, captures stdout to
separate files, and compares them with 'cmp -s'. Also compare exit codes. Print only
the mismatches, plus a final total of cases executed.

Generate inputs PROGRAMMATICALLY so you can cover hundreds to thousands of cases.
Use printf with escapes (e.g. printf '\xff') or python3 to build byte sequences, and
pass them via a shell array or python subprocess with a list argv — never by
re-splitting a string. python3 + subprocess.run([...], capture_output=True) with
bytes arguments (os.fsencode / bytes objects) is the most reliable route for
arbitrary bytes; prefer it.



Report every reproduced divergence with an exact repro command. If you find none,
say so honestly with divergenceCount 0 — a clean result is a useful result, and
inventing a finding is much worse than reporting none. In notes, state what you
deliberately did NOT cover so a later reviewer can pick it up.

content.text: Complete. 49,384 ASCII-focused differential cases, zero divergences, result reproduced twice with byte-identical logs.

input.strategy: ascii-exhaustive differential fuzzing via a perl fork/exec driver (no python3 on this image) at /tmp/wf-fuzz-r1-0/driver.pl and /tmp/wf-fuzz-r1-0/driver2.pl. Each case builds argv as a list of raw perl byte strings and execs both binaries directly (exec {$exe} ($exe,@args)) with no shell involved, so spaces, quotes, newlines and control bytes survive verbatim. stdout is captured over a pipe and compared byte-for-byte; wait status is compared as a raw integer (so both exit code and signal death would be caught). Any candidate mismatch is re-run a second time, persisted to /tmp/wf-fuzz-r1-0/mNNNN.{c,r}.out, and independently confirmed with `cmp -s`. Groups: (A) every single byte 0x01-0x7f; (B) all 16,129 two-byte combinations over 0x01-0x7f, not just printable; (C1) exhaustive 3-byte combos over a 21-char targeted alphabet ".aAzZxXnN-0 ~!_/%+" plus TAB and LF = 9,261; (C2) 4,000 pseudo-random printable 3-byte strings; (D) every byte 0x01-0x7f inserted at start, middle and end of 5 base strings ("abcdefgh.ijklmnop", "xn--exampl.com", "WWW.Example.COM.", "....", "xn--xn--Ab"); (E) ASCII length boundaries 0..4096; (F) multi-argv and empty-argument cases; (G1) exhaustive 4-byte over the ACE alphabet "xXnN-.aA" = 4,096; (G2) 12 xn-- prefixes and near-misses ("xn--","XN--","Xn--","xN--","xn-","xn---","xn--.","-xn--",...) crossed with every ASCII byte as prefix, suffix and both; (G3) exhaustive 5-byte over "xn-.A" = 3,125; (H) 4,800 random printable strings of length 1..24; (I) 2,400 random control-char-inclusive strings over 0x01-0x7f, length 1..16; (J) length boundaries 60-68 and 250-260 in five shapes; plus the no-argument fallback path and a 7-locale LC_ALL sweep. Harness soundness was proven with two negative controls (a wrapper that tr-mutates stdout, and one that returns exit 3): both fired MISMATCH on the very first case, confirming the driver detects stdout-byte and exit-code divergence rather than silently passing.
input.notes:
CLEAN RESULT — no divergence found in 49,384 cases. Round 1 (30,271 cases) was executed twice and the two logs are byte-identical (`cmp -s run1.log run1b.log` passes), so the clean outcome is deterministic, not a flake. Runtime ~1m53s per 30k-case pass.

Confidence checks I ran so the zero is trustworthy: (1) both negative controls fired immediately, so the comparator is not vacuously passing; (2) a sanity pass over 135 inputs confirmed the C++ binary produced non-empty stdout and exit 0 for every one, i.e. no case was "matching" because both binaries silently failed to exec; (3) the 4096-byte case produces 24,600 bytes of output on both sides and compares equal, so nothing is being truncated at a pipe boundary.

Surprising/notable, all matching: input "xn--" yields empty to_unicode and punycode_decode fields, so the line contains two runs of double spaces ("xn--xn--  xn--xn--  1 1 1 0 xn-- xn-- 1") — the port reproduces the collapsed-field formatting exactly. Case-sensitivity of the prefix strip is faithful: "XN--abc" is left intact by to_unicode while to_ascii lowercases it to "xn--xn--abc". The C++ program never calls setlocale, so ::tolower stays in the "C" locale; a sweep of LC_ALL=C/POSIX/C.UTF-8/en_US.UTF-8/tr_TR.UTF-8/de_DE.UTF-8/invalid matched on all seven, including the Turkish dotless-i locale that would be the classic place for a case-folding split.

DELIBERATELY NOT COVERED — for a later reviewer:
1. High bytes 0x80-0xff, multi-byte UTF-8, and invalid/truncated UTF-8. This is the big one and it is my angle's boundary, not an oversight. Because my whole corpus is <0x80, the is_ascii_domain and is_idn_domain fields were pinned at 1 and 0 for every single case — the IDN branch was never exercised. It is also where C++ is most likely to diverge: ::tolower(char) with a negative char argument is undefined behaviour in the C++ original, and the Rust port implements it as an unconditional byte-wise to_ascii_lowercase. Someone must fuzz 0x80-0xff, especially bytes 0xC0-0xDF followed by a byte in 0x41-0x5A (an 'A'-'Z'-valued UTF-8 continuation byte), to see whether the reference glibc ::tolower leaves it alone as the port assumes.
2. NUL (0x00) is untestable through this interface at all — execve terminates argv strings at NUL, so a 0x00 byte cannot reach either main(). Group A therefore starts at 0x01 by necessity, not by choice.
3. The >255-byte-but-<255-codepoint domain case called out in the Rust doc comment for is_valid_domain (e.g. 86 CJK characters = 258 bytes) needs non-ASCII input and is unverified.
4. stderr bytes were discarded to /dev/null; only stdout and wait status were compared. If either binary writes diagnostics to stderr, that difference is invisible to me.
5. Not stressed: ARG_MAX-scale single arguments (I stopped at 4096 bytes), large argv counts (max tested was 127 elements), and 4-byte-and-longer exhaustion over the full printable set (95^4+ was out of budget — I substituted targeted ACE-alphabet exhaustion plus random sampling, so an ASCII bug needing a specific 4+ byte combination outside the "xXnN-.aA0 ~!_/%+" alphabet could still be hiding).
